extracted.intended_audience: mathematics education researchers and undergraduate mathematics instructors
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and guidance for characterizing how students (and mathematicians) make sense of mathematical definitions, with a focused genetic decomposition (APOS) for the concepts of spanning set and span and observable behaviours linked to action/process/object/schema conceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decoding notation and supporting definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: When presented with an unfamiliar definition participants begin by sorting through specific terms and notations, requesting and receiving supporting definitions; understanding notation (and its implications) is central to situating the definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes noticing typesetting/notation differences, asking 'what is the definition of support', and testing connections to familiar contexts. Anti-pattern: overlooking notation subtleties (e.g., confusing interval vs ordered pair) can mislead sense-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situate definition within a mathematical setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians place a definition within a particular setting (previous definitions, notations, examples) to judge its value or usefulness; they need to know the purpose/context to evaluate generality and relevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a definition is presented outside familiar contexts participants first identify components to establish setting before using examples. Examples alone do not 'carry' the definition; one must know how the definition will be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of examples as a multi-faceted tool
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples are a key but not comprehensive tool for understanding definitions; they serve multiple roles rather than fully determining understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper identifies three facets (create shared experiences, develop precision, use test cases). Note participants often do not request examples immediately but rely on examples once context is clearer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples to create shared experiences
rubrics_metrics.description: Use examples to familiarize students with a concept through exploration, building intuition before formal definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples should engage students in exploration (e.g., leading through groups to highlight essential properties) so students acquire intuition prior to formal statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples to develop precision (including non-examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose examples (and crucially non-examples) to spotlight essential features of a definition and to develop learners' precision about which aspect of a definition fails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Participants recommend 'messy' examples and explicitly creating non-examples to reveal which part of the definition is not satisfied. Anti-pattern: only showing clean representative examples that hide boundary cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples as test cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a repertoire of familiar test objects to check whether they meet conditions of a definition and to expand understanding through repeated instantiation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experienced mathematicians acquire a 'list of standard examples' by practice and use these to test and generalize the definition's applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions should address purpose and be hierarchical
rubrics_metrics.description: Valued features of definitions include addressing the purpose for which they were invented and fitting into a hierarchical progression of concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when not explicitly stated by participants, attention to purpose and hierarchical structure appears implicit in their descriptions; teaching should reflect these features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understanding requires time and multiple focused processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians expect understanding of a definition to take time and to require focused attention on different aspects rather than instantaneous comprehension.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They ask targeted questions, consult resources when needed, and use multiple processes (decoding, connecting to contexts, examples) to build understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Action conception (APOS) — observable behaviours
rubrics_metrics.description: Students with an action conception perform step-by-step calculations or rely on memorized facts; they react to external cues providing precise steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In spanning-set context: can form linear combinations only by following explicit steps and can verify span only for specific example vectors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process conception (APOS) — observable behaviours
rubrics_metrics.description: Students with a process conception have interiorized transformations and can think about and describe them without executing every step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this domain: students can conceive of forming linear combinations as a coherent process and verify membership by reasoning about the process rather than executing full computations each time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Object conception (APOS) — observable behaviours
rubrics_metrics.description: Encapsulation of a process into an object: students treat the result as a mathematical object and can apply operations to it and de-encapsulate it back to the generating process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For spanning set: students who show object conception can treat a spanning set as an entity, explain different spanning sets for the same space, and decompose the notion back to linear combinations when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Schema coherence (APOS) — applicability criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A schema is a coherent collection of actions, processes, objects and related schemas; coherence is judged by the individual's ability to decide whether the schema applies in a situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment should check whether a learner can select and apply the schema appropriately to novel problem situations, not just perform isolated actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstractive reflection as transition mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitions between action→process→object are mediated by abstractive reflection, activated via physical or mental actions on knowledge objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction and assessment should provide tasks that promote reflective abstraction (e.g., varied instantiations, prompts to generalize) to foster transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite: vector space concept familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Students need to recognize familiar vector spaces (dimensions 1–3, n-tuples) and work flexibly with non-numeric vector spaces (polynomials, matrices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Teaching should ensure students can identify and operate within common vector spaces before tackling spanning set constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite: solution set as object (parametric representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should demonstrate an object conception of solution sets (ability to represent system solutions parametrically and describe geometric representations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is important because coordination with solving linear systems occurs when verifying whether a vector is a linear combination of a set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerequisite: variables as mathematical objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must treat variables flexibly (unknowns, general numbers, parameters) and move between these representations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fluency with variable interpretations supports forming and interpreting parametric descriptions of linear combinations and solution sets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process of forming linear combinations and finding scalars
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must perform scalar products and sums of vectors to form linear combinations and coordinate this with finding scalars (solution of resulting systems) to verify generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observable behavior: ability to set up and solve the system that yields scalars expressing a target vector as a combination of S; generalize across different instantiations of S and T.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encapsulation into spanning set and generated set objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Generalizing the process of verifying generation across instantiations leads to encapsulating that process into the object 'spanning set' and, conversely, 'spanned/generated set'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment: can the student treat spanning sets and spanned spaces as objects, recognize multiple spanning sets for a space, and reason about their relationships (cardinality not sole determinant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Observable indicators of action conception for spanning set
rubrics_metrics.description: A student has an action conception of spanning set if they use linear combination procedures only to verify specific vectors and cannot generalize to show the set spans the whole space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such students can demonstrate membership for particular examples but fail to produce general arguments or parametric descriptions showing full generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional sequencing: logical progression and shared experience
rubrics_metrics.description: When teaching, present ideas in a logical progression so students have the necessary pieces to understand definitions; create shared experiences through examples before formalization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design instruction that mirrors mathematicians' practices: provide supporting definitions/notations, sequenced examples (including messy/non-examples), and opportunities to use definitions in tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methodology for developing and validating genetic decompositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Research begins with a theoretical genetic decomposition modeling the epistemology of the target concept, then design an instrument to probe student constructions, test viability empirically, and refine the decomposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use students' work to refine the model and then employ the decomposition to guide teaching-material design; multiple decompositions may exist but must match observed student behaviour.
